title: Heat and Thermal Energy
description: Thermal energy is the total energy of moving particles in matter. Heat flows from warmer objects to cooler ones. Temperature measures how hot or cold something is.

exercises.question: What is TEMPERATURE a measure of?
choices: the total energy in an object
how hot or cold something is
how much water is in an object
exercises.exp: Temperature tells us how hot or cold something is — measured with a thermometer in degrees Celsius (°C).

exercises.question: Heat always flows from ___ to ___.
exercises.exp: Heat always flows from warmer objects to cooler ones — a hot cup of cocoa warms your cold hands!

exercises.question: A metal spoon in HOT soup gets warm. This shows ___.
choices: heat transferred from the soup to the spoon
exercises.exp: Heat flows from the hot soup into the cooler spoon — the spoon warms up!

exercises.question: What happens to particles when an object HEATS UP?
choices: they move faster and spread apart slightly
exercises.exp: Heating makes particles vibrate and move faster — this is why warm objects often expand slightly.

exercises.question: Which material is the BEST conductor of heat?
exercises.exp: Copper is an excellent thermal conductor — heat passes through it very quickly.

exercises.question: Which material is the BEST insulator (blocks heat)?
exercises.exp: Wool and foam trap air and slow heat transfer — great for keeping things warm or cold!

exercises.question: Why does ice cream MELT in your hand?
choices: your hand is cooler than the ice cream
heat flows from your warm hand to the cold ice cream
the ice cream heats your hand
ice cream melts on its own
exercises.exp: Your hand is warmer than the ice cream, so heat flows from your hand into the ice cream, melting it.

exercises.question: On a cold day, a metal railing FEELS colder than a wooden railing at the same temperature. Why?
choices: metal is actually colder than wood
metal conducts heat away from your hand faster
exercises.exp: Metal conducts heat quickly — it pulls heat away from your warm hand fast, so it feels colder!

exercises.question: What does a THERMOMETER measure?
exercises.exp: A thermometer measures temperature in degrees Celsius (°C) or Fahrenheit (°F).

exercises.question: Water boils at ___ °C.
exercises.exp: Water boils (becomes steam) at 100°C at sea level. It freezes at 0°C.

exercises.question: A thermos keeps soup HOT because it ___.
choices: blocks heat transfer with insulating walls
exercises.exp: A thermos has insulated walls that slow heat transfer — the soup stays hot for hours!

exercises.question: Which object has MORE thermal energy — a bathtub of warm water or a cup of boiling water?
choices: they have the same thermal energy
exercises.exp: Thermal energy depends on both temperature AND the number of particles. The bathtub has far more water particles, so more total thermal energy!

exercises.question: CONDUCTION is heat transfer through ___.
choices: direct contact between particles of matter
exercises.exp: Conduction happens when particles directly touch and transfer vibration energy — like a metal spoon heating in hot soup.

exercises.question: CONVECTION is heat transfer through ___.
choices: movement of heated fluids (liquids or gases)
exercises.exp: Convection is heat transfer by moving fluids. Hot air rises, cool air sinks, creating convection currents — like in a room with a heater!

exercises.question: RADIATION is heat transfer through ___.
choices: electromagnetic waves that can travel through empty space
exercises.exp: Radiation needs no medium — heat from the sun travels through the vacuum of space as electromagnetic waves (infrared radiation) to reach Earth!

exercises.question: When you hold your hands near (not touching) a CAMPFIRE and feel warmth, this is ___.
exercises.exp: The fire radiates infrared waves in all directions — you feel warmth without touching the fire or the air between you.

exercises.question: Hot air RISING from a heater and cool air SINKING is an example of ___.
exercises.exp: Heating air makes it less dense — it rises. Cooler, denser air sinks to replace it. This creates a convection current that distributes heat through a room.

exercises.question: A metal POT handle gets hot when placed on a stove. This is ___.
exercises.exp: Heat conducts through the metal pot and along the handle — direct particle-to-particle transfer (conduction).

exercises.question: Why are THERMOS FLASKS (vacuum flasks) so good at keeping drinks hot?
choices: they heat the drink using electricity
their vacuum walls stop conduction and convection; mirrored surfaces reduce radiation
they use magnets to trap heat
they add heat from the environment
exercises.exp: A thermos has a vacuum (no particles = no conduction/convection) and reflective walls (reduces radiation) — all three heat transfer methods blocked!

exercises.question: On a winter day, why does a metal BENCH feel colder than a wooden bench at the SAME temperature?
choices: wood is always warmer than metal
metal conducts heat away from your body much faster than wood
metal is colder than air temperature
wood has more particles than metal
exercises.exp: Metal is a great conductor — it quickly carries heat away from your warm skin, making it feel cold. Wood conducts poorly — it feels warmer!

exercises.question: DARK colours absorb more radiation than LIGHT colours. Which car gets HOTTER inside on a sunny day?
choices: they are all the same temperature
exercises.exp: Black absorbs most light and infrared radiation; white reflects it. A black car's interior heats up much more on a sunny day!

exercises.question: Fibre insulation is installed in WALLS and ROOFS of houses. What does it do?
choices: it conducts heat through walls faster
it traps air in tiny pockets, slowing heat transfer by conduction and convection
it blocks radiation from entering windows
exercises.exp: Fibreglass or wool insulation traps air — still air is a poor conductor. This slows heat loss in winter and heat gain in summer!

exercises.question: What is the UNIT used to measure temperature in most of the world?
exercises.exp: The Celsius scale (°C) is used worldwide in everyday life and science. Water freezes at 0°C and boils at 100°C.

exercises.question: A thermometer left in the sun reads a HIGHER temperature than one in the shade. Why?
choices: the sun creates a new substance in the thermometer
the thermometer in the sun absorbs more solar radiation, increasing its temperature
air is always hotter in sunlight
exercises.exp: Direct sunlight heats the thermometer via radiation — that is why weather stations keep thermometers in shaded, ventilated boxes for accurate air temperature readings.

exercises.question: When you add ice to a warm drink, the drink gets COOLER. What is actually happening?
choices: heat flows from the warmer drink to the colder ice, warming the ice and cooling the drink
the drink loses temperature on its own
the ice creates cold water which mixes in
exercises.exp: Heat always flows from hot to cold. Warmth from the drink flows into the cold ice, melting it and cooling the drink — equilibrium!

exercises.question: THERMAL EXPANSION means that ___.
choices: most materials expand (take up more space) when heated
water is the only substance that expands
exercises.exp: When heated, particles vibrate more and push farther apart — the material expands. Bridges and train tracks have expansion joints for this reason!

exercises.question: Why are EXPANSION JOINTS (small gaps) built into bridges and train tracks?
choices: to allow the metal to expand and contract with temperature changes without buckling
to reduce the weight of the bridge
exercises.exp: Metal expands in summer heat and contracts in winter cold. Without gaps for expansion, the structure would buckle and warp!

exercises.question: A POT OF SOUP is heated on a stove. Chunks of vegetable move around in the pot. This movement is caused by ___.
choices: convection currents in the liquid — hot liquid rises, cool liquid sinks
the vegetables floating on their own
exercises.exp: Convection currents in heated liquids carry food up and around — hot soup rises at the centre, cools at the edges, and sinks down.

exercises.question: The Earth's MOLTEN MANTLE flows very slowly due to ___.
choices: convection currents driven by heat from Earth's core
exercises.exp: Convection in the mantle drives tectonic plate movement — hot rock near the core rises, cools near the surface, then sinks back. This moves plates!

exercises.question: Why does hot AIR RISE?
choices: hot air is heavier than cold air
heating makes air expand and become less dense — less dense air is pushed upward by denser cold air
gravity reverses direction for hot air
exercises.exp: Hot air expands → lower density → buoyancy pushes it up (denser cold air falls to replace it). This drives convection and is why hot air balloons float!

exercises.question: A student wraps one hand in wool and leaves the other bare. She holds both near a hot lamp. Which hand feels less heat?
choices: the wool-covered hand — wool insulates and slows radiation/conduction
the wool-covered hand feels more heat
exercises.exp: Wool is an insulator — it slows heat transfer from the lamp to the hand, so the wool-covered hand stays cooler.

exercises.question: What is SPECIFIC HEAT CAPACITY?
choices: how hot an object gets when touched
the amount of energy needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1°C
how quickly a material conducts heat
exercises.exp: Specific heat capacity measures how much energy is needed to change a substance's temperature. Water has a very high specific heat — it resists temperature changes!

exercises.question: Heat always flows from ___.
choices: hot to cold — from higher temperature to lower temperature
exercises.exp: Heat always flows from hot to cold — from regions of higher temperature to lower temperature. This continues until thermal equilibrium is reached.

exercises.question: CONDUCTION happens mainly in ___.
choices: solids — especially metals where particles are close together and vibrate energy to neighbors
exercises.exp: Conduction works best in solids where tightly packed particles vibrate and pass energy to neighbors. Metals conduct especially well because free electrons carry energy.

exercises.question: CONVECTION transfers heat through ___.
choices: currents of moving fluid (liquid or gas) — warm fluid rises, cool fluid falls
exercises.exp: Convection: hot fluid becomes less dense → rises; cool fluid is denser → sinks. This creates convection currents that transfer heat through liquids and gases.

exercises.question: RADIATION transfers heat through ___.
choices: electromagnetic waves — no medium needed, can travel through vacuum
exercises.exp: Thermal radiation travels as electromagnetic waves (infrared). It does not need matter — sunlight warms Earth across 150 million km of empty space!

exercises.question: Why does a metal spoon in hot soup get warm quickly but a wooden spoon does not?
choices: metal is a good thermal conductor; wood is a poor conductor (insulator)
exercises.exp: Metal conducts heat rapidly from soup to your hand. Wood has very low thermal conductivity — it barely conducts heat at all. Safe to hold!

exercises.question: A THERMOS flask keeps drinks hot or cold using ___.
choices: a double-walled vacuum (reduces all three types of heat transfer: conduction, convection, radiation)
exercises.exp: Thermos design: vacuum between walls blocks convection & conduction; shiny silvered walls reflect radiation. All three transfer modes are minimized!

exercises.question: Why do COASTAL CITIES have milder climates than inland cities at the same latitude?
choices: water's high specific heat capacity moderates temperature — it heats up and cools down more slowly than land
coastal air is different from inland air
exercises.exp: Water's high specific heat means oceans change temperature slowly — releasing heat gradually in winter and staying cool in summer. Coastal cities benefit from this moderating effect!

exercises.question: A black car and a white car sit in the same sunny car park. Which interior gets hotter?
choices: the black car — dark colours absorb more solar radiation
exercises.exp: Black surfaces absorb more radiation (and convert it to heat). White surfaces reflect more. Black cars absorb more sunlight → hotter interior!

exercises.question: THERMAL EQUILIBRIUM is reached when ___.
choices: two objects in contact reach the same temperature and heat stops flowing between them
one object gains all the heat
exercises.exp: Thermal equilibrium: heat flows until both objects are the same temperature — then net heat transfer stops. A cold drink warms up until it matches room temperature.

exercises.question: The unit of TEMPERATURE is degrees Celsius (°C). The unit of HEAT ENERGY is ___.
exercises.exp: Temperature is in °C (or Kelvin). Heat energy is measured in joules (J). Power (energy per second) is in watts. Food energy is in kilojoules (kJ).

exercises.question: Hot air RISES because ___.
choices: hot air is lighter (less dense) than cool air — buoyancy causes it to rise
the sun attracts hot air particles upward
exercises.exp: Heating air makes it expand → less dense → lighter than surrounding cooler air → rises (buoyancy). This drives convection currents in atmosphere and oceans!

exercises.question: Why do we feel COLD when we get out of a swimming pool on a windy day?
choices: wind pushes us away from the warm pool
water on our skin evaporates, and wind speeds up evaporation — evaporation absorbs heat from our skin
cold wind adds cold particles to our skin
exercises.exp: Wind accelerates evaporation of water from your skin. Evaporation is endothermic — absorbs heat from skin. More evaporation = more heat removed = colder!

exercises.question: Engineers use FINS on computer processors to cool them. Fins work by ___.
choices: increasing the surface area for convection — more surface area means faster heat loss to air
being magnetic and attracting heat away
exercises.exp: Heat sink fins massively increase surface area — more surface touching air = faster convection heat transfer away from the hot processor. Essential for computers!

exercises.question: What happens to molecules when a solid EXPANDS with heat?
choices: molecules vibrate faster and push each other apart slightly — the object becomes slightly larger
exercises.exp: Heat makes particles vibrate more vigorously — they push each other slightly further apart. The object's overall size increases. This is thermal expansion!

exercises.question: EXPANSION JOINTS are gaps left in bridges and railway tracks. Why?
choices: to allow the material to expand with heat in summer without buckling or breaking
to allow water to drain through
exercises.exp: Metals expand when hot and contract when cold. Expansion joints give room for this movement — without them, summer heat would buckle bridges and rails!

exercises.question: The KELVIN scale starts at absolute zero. What is 0°C in Kelvin?
exercises.exp: 0°C = 273.15 K. To convert °C to Kelvin, add 273. Absolute zero = 0 K = −273°C. Water boils at 373 K = 100°C!

exercises.question: A central heating RADIATOR heats a room mainly by ___.
choices: convection — air near the hot radiator warms up, rises, and circulates heat throughout the room
all heat transfer is blocked by the radiator's colour
exercises.exp: Despite the name 'radiator', most room heating is by convection — warm air rises from the hot radiator and circulates. Some radiation occurs but convection dominates.

exercises.question: Which of these has the HIGHEST specific heat capacity (is hardest to heat up)?
exercises.exp: Water has a specific heat of 4.18 J/g°C — much higher than metals. It takes 4.18 joules to raise 1g of water by 1°C. That is why oceans moderate Earth's climate!

exercises.question: What is a HEAT PUMP (like an air conditioner)?
choices: a device that creates heat from nothing
a device that moves heat from one place to another using work (electricity) — from cold to hot
a device that stores heat in batteries
a device that converts heat to light
exercises.exp: A heat pump transfers heat against its natural direction (from cold to hot) using energy input. An air conditioner moves heat from inside (cool) to outside (warm)!
